source_terms: You need to make your product or service more expensive than the competition.
You need to find a code word for prestige.
item.claim: Where the word a brand wants to own is prestige, the authors say the word itself cannot be used, because people want prestige brands but will not admit it. They give a two-part procedure: price the product substantially above the comparable competitor, and find a code word that lets the buyer justify the purchase on other grounds. Their case is Mercedes-Benz, priced at about twice a comparable Cadillac, with an engineering line standing in for the prestige claim and giving the owner an excuse to buy an expensive car.

mechanism.text: Two mechanisms combine. Price is read as evidence — the buyer infers that a car costing twice as much must be better. The code word handles the social problem that the real motive cannot be stated aloud, so the brand supplies a defensible reason for a purchase made on another one.

scope.conditions: specific to prestige as the target attribute

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. In a diaspora territory whose audience does not hold that system, removing the text removes the signal and does not replace it, and the source says nothing about what would. Nothing here is measured either: no comparison of a text-carrying and a text-free poster is reported anywhere in the book.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: Treating this as a minimalist design principle inverts it. The convention is a distribution constraint, and in a single-language market the constraint is absent.

results.representation_note: Q&A is an alternate grounded representation of the same source. It corroborates nothing on its own.

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', sections 'Can your brand own something visual?' and 'Avoid style. Focus on substance.' (spine 15)
item.question: Sullivan endorses Krone's twenty-foot test and then makes a stronger claim of his own. State both, and identify the tension between this and his instruction to study a category's current visual conventions.
item.answer: Krone's requirement is a page style: you should be able to tell whose advertisement it is from a distance of twenty feet — and Sullivan notes what is interesting about it, which is that Krone was talking about print advertisements, not billboards. Sullivan's stronger claim is that the longer he is in the business the more convinced he is that art direction is where the major battle for brand building happens, because once a look is established and a design territory staked out, nobody else can use it without looking like your brand. He pairs it with an instruction to pull the look from the brand's own DNA rather than from current fashion, since riding every passing fad makes work trendy and derivative. The tension: knowing and avoiding a category's current clichés requires close attention to exactly the conventions this instruction says to ignore. He states both and does not reconcile them.
item.support: Krone is quoted from a 1968 trade interview; the stronger claim is Sullivan's own opinion, flagged by his phrasing, with no evidence. The colour-ownership examples are assertions about market perception with nothing measuring them. The tension is an extractor observation.
confounders: treating the twenty-foot test as calibrated; no viewing condition is specified
reading 'avoid style' as indifference to craft rather than as a warning against period fashion
assuming ownership of a colour or a look is established rather than asserted

a dramatic enigma
the media seal of approval
item.claim: Patel states a structural contrast between two poster traditions. Contemporary Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which requires the public to see the film to resolve it, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as "the media seal of approval," plus studio, producer and director credits that signal the film's status. Indian posters, in contrast, "rarely use text": with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, "text is seen as a cultural barrier." From the 1980s onward it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are a marker of the style, content and quality of the film. Indian posters accordingly "convey the familiarity of the form and content of the Indian film" rather than an enigma.

mechanism.text: Text has to be read in a language, so any text narrows the poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory. Where the distribution is wide and the audience already knows the form, the poster's job shifts from posing a question to confirming a familiar promise, and that job can be done by images and by three names.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters from the 1980s onward against contemporary Western practice. Patel notes the earlier Indian convention was different — title and star names prominently in English with Hindi and Urdu titles in smaller lettering nearby — so this too is dated.

caveats.text: the comparison is drawn between two practices as the author characterises them; no sample of Western posters is enumerated and no count is given on either side

Patel notes the cost of the change she documents: more recent designs focusing on one narrative element are 'more universally understood' but 'convey less information about the culture in which they are produced'. That trade-off is stated by the source and is the most useful part of this object

source_stated_problems: text narrows a poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory
source_stated_remedies: carry the message in recognisable images and in the three names that index style, content and quality

positive: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995), three posters each focusing on a strand of the romance
Pardes (1997), an amalgamation with an American cityscape and the Taj Mahal diagonally opposed

source_terms: This represents a dramatic shift in compositional emphasis, from emphatically horizontal—in which the verticality of the columns adds contrast—to overtly vertical, in which row divisions assume an increased level of importance.
it’s important that strong horizontal breaks and alignments of a similar quality as will appear in the small format are built into the large format presentation to ensure continuity
item.claim: Material placed in the rightward columns of a large-screen layout reorients into a single-column vertical scroll when the browser closes to smartphone width. That is a dramatic inversion of compositional emphasis: from emphatically horizontal, where the columns' verticality supplies contrast, to overtly vertical, where the row divisions become far more important. A change this pronounced can disunify a branded experience, so horizontal breaks and alignments of the same quality as those that will appear in the small format must be built into the large-format presentation to preserve continuity.

mechanism.text: Collapsing several columns into one removes the horizontal reading and leaves only the vertical, so whatever the layout's character depended on horizontally has to be carried by the rows instead.

scope.conditions: responsive layouts that collapse to a single column

caveats.text: the remedy asks the designer to compromise the large-format composition in advance for the sake of a small-format one that does not exist yet

source_stated_problems: a layout change pronounced enough to disunify a branded experience
source_stated_remedies: build strong horizontal breaks and alignments into the large-format layout to match those the small format will produce

intra_source_relations.note: what happens at the extremes of the range

source_terms: Centered-Axis Structure
centering is structurally antithetical to grid-based visualization

because it assumes only one governing alignment axis; because that axis is "buried" within the area of the material, rather than marked by its contours; and because the exterior contours, widths, and depths of centered elements are mutually interdependent
a sense of immediacy, or unfussy directness
item.claim: Centred-axis, or symmetrical, composition arranges elements in response to the format's centre — halfway between left and right or top and bottom edges, and sometimes in response to each other's central axes independently of the format. Although a grid may guide the proportions or positions of centred material, centring is structurally antithetical to grid-based visualisation, for three stated reasons: it assumes only one governing alignment axis; that axis is buried inside the area of the material rather than marked by its contours; and the exterior contours, widths and depths of centred elements are mutually interdependent — driven by their fit and relative proportion as they come into central alignment, not by predetermined intervals. Elements stack sequentially top to bottom or left to right, and the shapes either side of the axis, and the negative spaces beyond them, are identical. The primary visual result is a sense of immediacy or unfussy directness, followed by an appearance of formal simplicity, as the material's quality as a unit dominates perception of its internal divisions.

mechanism.text: A grid works by predetermined intervals marked at the contours of the material; a centred axis works by mutual fit around a line that is not drawn. The two allocate space by incompatible logics, which is why one cannot simply be laid over the other.

scope.conditions: classical or traditional page architecture, print or screen

caveats.text: Samara calls this the classical or traditional page architecture, so the claim is partly a statement about a Western typographic convention rather than about perception.
This is an unusual member of a chapter about breaking grids: the alternative here is older than the grid, not newer.

positive.description: a poster whose typographic and planar image forms situate around the format's central vertical axis while the title reads across both vertical and horizontal axes

item.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Layouts', the news-magazine format passage (spine 13)
item.question: What does Ogilvy claim the conventional graphics of advertising communicate to a reader before a word is read, and what does he propose in their place?
item.answer: He claims the inherited graphic conventions of advertising telegraph to the reader that this is only an advertisement and can be skipped, and reports that roughly six times as many people read the average article as the average advertisement while very few advertisements are read by more than one reader in twenty. His proposal is to adopt editorial graphics instead: copy given priority over illustration, serif type, three columns of thirty-five to forty-five characters, a caption under every photograph, drop-initials, and black type on white. His instruction is to pretend you are an editor. The whole argument depends on a specific historical relationship between editorial and advertising conventions in the print of his period.
item.support: Stated claim with a reported article-to-advertisement readership ratio, no source given. The six-element list is his description of the format shared by named news magazines in five countries.
confounders: reading it as a preference for restraint or good taste; his claim is about a learned signal that triggers skipping
carrying the specific format list into any later medium; it describes printed magazines of 1983
confusing 'looks like editorial' with disguising the advertiser — he wants the graphics, and separately jokes about the required 'advertisement' slug

source_terms: bilateral
rotational symmetry

Symmetry is described as bilateral (left) if form elements' centers align with the axis, straddling it, as well as mirror each other across the axis. In rotational symmetry (middle), elements invert in their orientation relative to the axis.
item.claim: The source distinguishes three symmetrical arrangements by name. Symmetry is bilateral when form elements' centres align with the axis, straddling it, and mirror each other across it. It is rotational when elements invert in their orientation relative to the axis. Arranging forms symmetrically around two axes creates greater complexity. Elements or groups may respond to a format's vertical, horizontal or diagonal axis.

caveats.text: This is terminology attached to a diagram. The words are recorded because the vocabulary is the reusable part; the diagram that distinguishes the three cases visually was not seen, and no further distinction is inferred from the sentence.
